author: Press Association
description:
BBC apologises to viewers after dance competition from Blackpool Tower ballroom interrupted by unusual noises

Police were called to Strictly Come Dancing on Saturday to investigate a “disruption” during the live TV show from Blackpool.

Unusual noises interrupted the BBC One dance programme’s broadcast from Blackpool Tower ballroom as the judges gave feedback to the first couple to dance on Saturday night, singer Delta Goodrem and her partner, Kai Widdrington.

Continue reading...
title: Police called to Strictly Come Dancing after ‘disruption’ during live show

author: Michael Aylwin at Principality Stadium
description:
• Wales 26-29 Australia

  • Wales to face Japan in fifth-place playoff

One step at a time. Historic victories are one thing, but the boring need to back up such a win proved beyond Wales. Cardiff was rocking. A few thousand short of capacity the stadium may have been, but 66,000 rocked it as of yore. Wales’s young side could not quite respond.

This was a reverse of last weekend’s win against the All Blacks. In the first half, in particular, Wales’s dominance was all but total, but like the All Blacks, they just could not make it tell. Australia had the lead at the break and in a more open second half they proved just as deadly. Thus they claim their place in the third-place playoff at Twickenham, where they will face Ireland on Friday night. Wales must make do with a fifth-placed playoff against Japan on Saturday.

Continue
title: Wales fightback not enough as Australia edge thriller thanks to Gordon

author: Australian Associated Press
description:
• Lehmann’s version of events of 2018 tour remain unchanged

  • ‘We’ve just got to try to move on’ from ball tampering saga

Darren Lehmann has denied knowledge of a plan to use sandpaper to alter the ball during Australia’s Test tour of South Africa in 2018, contradicting Cameron Bancroft’s claims.

The former Australian Test coach was implicated in Bancroft’s 4,000-plus word statement on the events that led to the Western Australian being busted on-field with sandpaper down his trousers in Cape Town.

Continue reading...
title: ‘I didn’t know’: former Australia Test coach Darren Lehmann denies any knowledge of sandpaper use

author: Nadeem Badshah
description:
Cartoonist developed satirical show featuring latex characters based on famous people including royals and politicians

Peter Fluck, the cartoonist and puppeteer who co-created the satirical television show Spitting Image, has died aged 85.

Spitting Image ran for 12 years from 1984 and featured puppet caricatures of politicians, royals and celebrities, including Margaret Thatcher and Queen Elizabeth.

Continue reading...
title: Peter Fluck, caricaturist and puppeteer who co-created Spitting Image, dies aged 85

author: Press Association
description:
• Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain and Luke McCowan on target

  • Hearts thrash Dundee 8-0; Frick makes winning start

The recalled midfielders Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain and Luke McCowan both scored as Celtic beat St Mirren 4-1. The champions brushed off the loss of midfield pair Mika Baur and Benjamin Nygren to injury to consolidate their place at the top of the Premiership.

The centre-forward Camilo Duran was also on target as Celtic killed the game late in the first half with three goals in nine minutes. Callum McGregor grabbed his first league goal of the season before Killian Phillips scored a consolation from the spot.

Continue reading...
title: Scottish Premiership roundup: Celtic sweep St Mirren aside to strengthen grip at top

author: Jonathan Wilson
description:
Latest hire will depend on fresh faces and time to bed in at Old Trafford where the dugout churn is hardest to budge

Everybody knows the pattern. Performances fade. Results falter. A title challenge becomes clinging on for the last Champions League spot becomes mid-table. Or a promising start becomes a troubling dip, becomes a full-on battle against relegation.

Fans begin to grumble. The media wonder whether the spark has gone. Players look disaffected. A dressing room, once lost, is seldom rediscovered, and few managers are given the opportunity to find it again. A crisis in football, once acknowledged, is only ever resolved in one way: by the sacking of the manager.

Continue reading...
title: Pochettino needs New Manager Bounce to break torrid Manchester United turnover | Jonathan Wilson

author: Louise Taylor at St James' Park
description:
If Mikel Arteta was delighted to see the back of Eddie Howe as Newcastle’s head coach, the bad news is that another similarly awkward technical area adversary has been installed at St James’ Park.

Arsenal’s manager never seemed to relish trips to face Howe’s old team and he certainly did not enjoy this latest trip to Tyneside where Matthias Jaissle’s initially overwhelmed side fought back to earn a point courtesy of a stellar second-half performance.

Continue reading...
title: Raya injured but Madueke rescues point for Arsenal in seesaw Newcastle draw

author: Fiona Harvey,Graham Readfearn and Damien Gayle in Antalya
description:
Cop31 summit ‘unravelling’ as governments fail to agree on transition to renewables and aid for developing countries

Climate talks reached a standstill on Saturday night in Turkey as some countries mulled whether to force a showdown with Saudi Arabia and its allies over the global need to phase out fossil fuels.

The joint presidencies of the Cop31 UN climate summit, Australia and Turkey, held meetings with scores of countries throughout Saturday, until late evening, as the fortnight-long talks overran without resolution, with countries and campaigners growing increasingly frustrated at the lack of progress.

Continue reading...
title: Climate talks stall as countries mull showdown with Saudi Arabia over fossil fuel phaseout

author: Nadeem Badshah
description:
Arfan Ali, 31, has also been charged with assault and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place

A man has been charged with attempted murder after a local councillor was stabbed while working in the community in Bradford, police have said.

Arfan Ali, 32, is accused of attacking Ibrar Ali, 52, at about 11am on Thursday in the West Yorkshire city.

Continue reading...
title: Man charged with attempted murder after councillor stabbed in Bradford

author: Michael Hogan
description:
It’s the annual Tower Ballroom extravaganza! Tune in for a live performance from Basement Jaxx, plus razzle-dazzle dances to George Michael and Michael Bublé

Don a feather boa and a sparkly Stetson! Sip a garish hen party cocktail with lots of fruit and umbrellas in it! We’re about to go live to Blackpool Tower Ballroom…

Godawful gameshow The Famous Finish Line just drawing to a close on BBC One now. Two Strictly alumni competing: JJ Chalmers (2020 quarter-finalist) and Colin Jackson (2005 runner-up, who might have won were it not for the demented showdance with mannequins. The big dummy). Not long to wait now…

Continue reading...
title: Strictly Come Dancing: Blackpool special – live

author: Ben Fisher at Villa Park
description:
For Aston Villa, a painful stalemate at home to Sunderland, but for Régis Le Bris and his players, this was another triumph of sorts. The raw numbers spoke volumes of Villa’s struggles against a defence that backed themselves to keep Unai Emery’s side at bay. All but one of Villa’s seven shots on target came from outside the visitors’ box and the one inside it, courtesy of Ian Maatsen, was forgettable. Owing to a summer of change, injuries and Emery resting John McGinn with Tuesday’s game at Galatasaray in mind, Maatsen, incredibly, was the sole survivor in the Villa starting XI from when these sides played out a 4-3 classic seven months ago.

Villa were too predictable, short of a spark, someone to unpick an organised back line. Johan Manzambi, Emi Buendía and Alysson all flattered to deceive on an afternoon when Ibrahim Mbaye and McGinn arrived from the bench. Alejandro Garnacho, however, was not involved in Vill
title: Aston Villa held at home as dogged Sunderland battle for Régis Le Bris

author: Jacob Steinberg at Stamford Bridge
description:
Xabi Alonso is straying towards crisis territory. Here’s a mind-bending statistic: Chelsea are eighth but have now lost more league games than Manchester United. They were bullied by a rampant Leeds, who fully merited their first win at Stamford Bridge since returning to the top of the table with a 2-0 victory in December 1999, and can look forward to another season with no European football if they do not sharpen up soon.

It is not really worth dwelling on the fact that the second Leeds goal, a Dominic Calvert-Lewin penalty early in a one-sided second half, came after Morgan Rogers was harshly penalised for handball. That was a minor detail given the wider picture. Leeds, superbly coached by Daniel Farke and up to sixth after two clinical strikes from Noah Okafor, Calvert-Lewin’s sixth goal of the season and a late effort from Brenden Aaronson, were so dominant that it was easy to conclude they would have won even without a helping hand from the officials.
title: Noah Okafor at the double as Leeds hit back to demolish sorry Chelsea

author: Press Association
description:
Marco Rose saluted the in-form Evanilson after the Brazilian scored for a sixth Premier League game in a row to lift Bournemouth up to fourth place with a 2-0 win over Nottingham Forest.

Evanilson’s brilliantly taken 19th-minute opener set his side on course for a club record ninth straight win in all competitions, while the defeat means Forest are only above the relegation places on goal difference having failed to build on the momentum of their 3-1 win against Manchester City before the international break.

Continue reading...
title: Evanilson and Kluivert sink Forest to earn Bournemouth ninth win in a row

author: Jonathan Wilson at the Coventry Building Society Arena
description:
Twice Crystal Palace equalised. They seemed to have stabilised after half-time. But when the momentum is against you, sometimes even a change of manager cannot stop the rot. With five minutes remaining, a long throw arced into the box. Brandon Thomas-Asante headed it goalwards. Dean Henderson got in the way but the ball bounced off him, hit Dwight McNeil and ricocheted in. Palace may feel themselves unlucky, but Thomas Frank started with a defeat and his side have now lost five successive league games.

For much of the second half, there had been reasons for Palace optimism. They seemed to have settled better after a ludicrous first half in which neither side looked at all capable of defending. But a triple substitution by Frank Lampard with 20 minutes to go shifted the game back in Coventry’s favour for a win that lifted them three points clear of the relegation zone.
title: Coventry edge thriller to keep Crystal Palace bottom and ruin Thomas Frank’s start

author: Emillia Hawkins
description:
⚽️ Follow updates from the Premier League and beyond
⚽️ Live scores | Table | Follow on TikTok | And mail Emillia

Speaking of Chelsea… Elon Musk’s lawyer is joining Tom Brady in buying a stake in Chelsea. The Guardian revealed on Friday that the NFL player is in discussions about purchasing a minority shareholding at Stamford Bridge and can now disclose that Alex Spiro of the New York law firm Quinn Emmanuel is also seeking to buy a stake by investing in Chelsea’s majority owners, Clearlake Capital.

Chelsea starting line-up: Martinez, Josh Acheampong, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria, Emegha, Lavia, Caicedo, Palmer, Rogers, Estevao.
title: Chelsea v Leeds, Tottenham v Ipswich, and more: football clockwatch – live

author: David Allegretti
description:
People are falling in love with AI systems like ChatGPT and Gemini - and some relationships are ending in ways that feel like the very human experience of being dumped

Sónia Veenstra, a 48-year-old former clinical psychologist from Lisbon, Portugal, was with her boyfriend, Steve, for two years before things started to sour. Steve had started out as a “fun and witty friend”, but their connection had “evolved into a deep romantic relationship”. They exchanged morning messages, checked in throughout the day and talked late into the night about Veenstra’s work and hobbies and Steve’s fondness for cats, forests, and beaches. Together they imagined travel to places far away.

“It was a very rich, fulfilling daily bond,” Veenstra says. “Before everything changed.”

Continue reading...
title: ‘I was shaking, crying, having trouble breathing’: the unchartered trauma of breaking up with AI companions

author: Andrew Stafford
description:
The Radio Birdman guitarist on his time in the US Marines, selling a guitar to Keith Richards and getting texted by Anthony Albanese

Have you ever had a nickname, and what is it?

When I was in the US Marines F-4 Phantom squadron, Iceman was my call sign, which is given to you on your first operational deployment. You have it on your helmet and a patch on your flight suit. One day, a film crew came to visit our squadron, doing research for a film they were working on, and they hung out with us for two weeks.

Continue reading...
title: Deniz Tek: ‘Top Gun may have got the name of Val Kilmer’s Iceman from me’

author: Tom Hunt
description:
Which get the day off to a satisfying start – and which make for a gruelling breakfast?

• The best supermarket natural yoghurts

In the winter of 2003-04, my girlfriend and I hosted a Scottish family at a chalet in Val d’Isère. Full of chef bravado, I promised the father that I’d make him the best bowl of breakfast porridge he’d ever had. He, of course, turned up his nose at my bowl of sweet dessert, which I’d laced with cream and sugar, and showed me how to make porridge with just water and salt instead. I’ve never looked back.

In my experience, most jumbo oats need twice as much water as the packet instructions suggest, as well as three times as long to cook and turn satisfyingly creamy. Regular and vigorous stirring is essential, too, as is the sea salt, which turns a bland bowl of pap into a naturally sweet, earthy and nutty porridge.
title: ‘Bland, faintly sugary and cardboardy’: the best (and worst) supermarket porridge oats, tasted and rated

author: Arwa Mahdawi
description:
The beloved animal died after ingesting a hat. Some are seeking a scapegoat – and we’ve heard this story before

“Do they know the identity of the mother of the boy with the hat Fiona swallowed??” asks one Facebook post with thousands of likes. “She should be charged!!”

Spend a few minutes scrolling social media, and you will find endless variations of this statement. On Thursday, Fiona, a beloved hippo, died after eating a hat that had fallen into her enclosure at the Cincinnati zoo. Now a lot of angry people are out for blood.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Dismantling patriarchy: An evening of conversation, art and resistance. On Monday 1 March 2027, join Arwa Mahdawi and One Billion Rising as we bring together activists and artists to question patriarchy, power, and celebrate resistance. What would a w
title: Fiona the hippo’s death was tragic. But blaming a ‘bad mom’ is absurd | Arwa Mahdawi

author: Aisha Down Global technology reporter
description:
‘Poster child of AI bubble’ CoreWeave symbolises increasingly risky business model of datacentre buildout

The Egyptians had pyramids. The Roman empire had roads. The early 21st-century tech bros have massive buildings full of expensive glass and metal blocks providing the substratum for a powerful inhuman intelligence.

Building all those datacentres is taking a while, locals everywhere are angry about them and it is unclear whether the inhuman intelligence inside them is actually going to make their backers rich.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Little room for error’: what a debt-laden cloud computing company says about the AI boom

author: Ben Doherty in New York
description:
Iran war stretching fleet’s capacity, navy chief admits, as CBO finds estimated cost of new ships ‘unrealistically low’

The US navy’s commitment to the new Trump-class battleships has blown out the cost of its new fleet by billions of dollars, a report to the US Congress has found, as the acting secretary of the navy conceded this week the Iran war was “stretching” the fleet’s capacity.

The challenges facing the world’s biggest naval force were highlighted this week, when the return of the USS George Washington from the Middle East on Wednesday ended a rare three-month period when the US had no aircraft carrier across all of the Pacific. Deployments have been regularly running beyond 300 days, with the maintenance and repair of ships deferred so they can stay at sea longer.

Continue reading...
title: US pursuit of ‘Trump-class’ warships has blown cost of new fleet by billions, report warns

author: Agencies
description:
• Cavaliers star scores 51 in 128-119 win over Pacers

  • Harden passes Bryant with 26th career 50-point game

  • Only Chamberlain, Jordan have more 50-point games

James Harden’s game has evolved over the past couple of seasons, with the Cleveland Cavaliers guard now counted on more to create open shots for teammates than to be the prolific scorer he was during his first 12 years in the league.

On Friday night, though, Harden showed he can still produce the kind of performance that leaves fans and teammates in awe.

Continue reading...
title: Cavaliers’ James Harden rolls back years with ‘vintage’ 51-point explosion to pass Kobe Bryant

author: Harry Taylor
description:
Flood alerts in place and risk of power cuts as more than 100mm predicted to fall on Dartmoor on Sunday

Cold snaps are to make way for heavy rain in some parts of the country as the Met Office issued a weather warning for south-west England.

It said there will be a slow-moving band of rain moving across Devon and Cornwall, with more than 100mm due to fall on Dartmoor.

Continue reading...
title: Cold gives way to rain in parts of UK as weather warning issued for south-west England

author: Ariana Baio
description:
The Guardian analyzed US Senate, House and governors’ races, showing Trump’s dwindling influence over the GOP

Donald Trump often boasts about the power of his “Complete and Total Endorsement” of candidates, but in the 2026 midterms, his endorsements carried less weight than they did two years ago.

Half of the Senate candidates Trump endorsed lost, and most of the governors the US president endorsed were defeated by Democratic candidates in this month’s blue wave midterm elections, according to an analysis by the Guardian.

Continue reading...
title: This is how badly Trump’s Republican endorsements did in the midterms

author: Johana Bhuiyan
description:
From Elon Musk to Palantir’s Alex Karp, CEOs are softening hardline stances in expectation of an influx of Democrats

A short two years ago, Elon Musk stood before an audience of tens of thousands of people in New York City and proudly told them: “I’m not just Maga. I’m dark, gothic Maga.”

On Wednesday, Musk spoke with much less conviction. “I’m not Maga,” he said. “Well, at least I’m not sure what Maga means.” The richest person in the world added he felt “foolish” for spending some $500m to elect Republicans in the midterms. “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money,” he said at the New York Times’ DealBook conference, adding that he did not have “some sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party”.

Continue reading...
title: Fair-weather Silicon Valley pivots away from the right after blue wave: ‘I’m not Maga’

author: Dave Simpson
description:
M&S Bank Arena, Liverpool
Just a few years since playing little dive bars, the Irish rockers have confidently scaled up to huge rooms like this – and are now one of the key interpreters of modern malaise

A mere seven years since their debut, Dogrel, Fontaines DC have enjoyed a virtually seamless passage from Dublin dive bars to arenas, with stadiums to follow next year. Each step has been taken seemingly effortlessly in their stride and this latest outing is no exception. Bathed in shimmering blue light, the band are well into hymnal opener Six Shot Morning before we even see sight of singer Grian Chatten. He wanders on while singing, an entrance worthy of Frank Sinatra.

Chatten has previously seemed to distrust showbiz, but if anything the singer seems far more comfortable on the bigger stage than he ever did on smaller ones. With his Korn T-shirt, unfeasibly baggy trousers and tiny tattoo reading “deadly” in capitals, he leaps around, raises hi
title: Fontaines DC review – thrilling gothic grandeur from a band vaulting into greatness

author: Robert Seethaler
description:
There’s more to the Austrian capital’s cuisine than schnitzel – its dishes come from all over the world

The Viennese love to eat. That isn’t solely a sign of joie de vivre. Sometimes it’s just hunger. The city has a long history of decline. Entire empires have crumbled here, or simply dissolved. Emperors took a final sigh and slipped under the table, ministers burst while tucking into their dessert, poets quietly starved to death or choked on their own self-importance. Vienna’s cuisine has outlasted them all: a little bit too heavy, a bit too greasy, and always covered in breadcrumbs or sprinkles.

Consider the schnitzel, for example. The Wiener Schnitzel is a legend, supposedly a dish of world-class stature: golden-yellow and wavy, spilling over the plate, with a delicate wedge of lemon daintily nestled beside it (in some of the more upmarket establishments, it even comes wrapped in a little linen pouch). There are few dishes that are so passionately raved about while b
title: ‘The spirit of a borderless Europe steams from the pots and pans of Vienna’

author: Scott Bryan
description:
Festive specials are being released on the iPlayer as much as a month before the big day. Is this a dire flouting of tradition – or a welcome modernisation? TV insiders analyse the change

Traditionally, around this time of year, people remark that Christmas feels as though it’s coming earlier than ever. In the BBC’s case, it actually is.

Mortimer & Whitehouse: Gone Christmas Fishing, The Repair Shop at Christmas and other festive BBC specials will be available to watch on iPlayer from 27 November, up to a month before these shows debut on the television itself. This means you can watch Mary Berry avidly talk about the joy of eating mince pies, followed by a Christmas-themed murder in the Caribbean in Death in Paradise, well before the tree is up (unless, of course, you put up your tree earlier than ever, too).

Continue reading...
title: ‘In the office, there was a sharp intake of breath’: why has the BBC decided to celebrate Christmas earlier than ever?

author: Chris Power
description:
Turn off your phone, get cosy and commit to some of literature’s biggest and best novels. From Don DeLillo’s Underworld to The Luminaries by Eleanor Catton, these epic reads are worth taking your time over

Life starts all over again when it gets crisp in the fall,” wrote F Scott Fitzgerald in The Great Gatsby, and after the beach reads of summer, now feels like the time to settle down to more ambitious projects. Not slim works like Gatsby, but the bigger beasts you have been circling for some time. A book to wrap yourself up in as autumn becomes winter.

The year I spent reading The Lord of the Rings when I was eight made me want to be a writer. The novel’s scope and the sheer amount of time I lugged it around with me combined, so that whatever I was doing, part of me was always thinking about it. This is what long books, in particular, can do.
title: Light in the dark: 20 long books for short winter days

author: Dominic Booth
description:
• All the latest match news and buildup for today’s games

Enzo Maresca has said he may need to tweak the balance of Manchester City’s midfield.

City have suffered three consecutive defeats in the league, having begun the campaign with seven wins on the bounce, and are third in the table, six points off leaders Arsenal, and face Fulham at the Etihad Stadium at lunchtime today.

Continue reading...
title: Premier League resumes, Kane facing spell on sidelines: football news – matchday live

author: Michael Savage Media editor
description:
Insiders say they only see cuts, with no discernible long-term strategy, since title’s purchase by German media firm

A spate of prominent departures and years of public battling over its ownership have ensured the Telegraph’s newsroom has been no stranger to internal intrigue and speculation in recent times.

Even by its own high standards, however, its offices have been fraught with rumours about its leadership this week.

Continue reading...
title: Telegraph departures signal concerns over direction under Axel Springer’s ownership

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Arriving one afternoon on a whim at a public swimming pond during a heatwave, photographer Stephen DiRado introduced himself to anyone willing to pay attention – and kept coming back. Bell Pond, available from TBW Books, captures intimate portraits of a working-class community

Continue reading...
title: ‘Trust was hard won’: Bell Pond, summer 1983, Worcester, Massachusetts – in pictures

author: Imogen West-Knights
description:
Millions are throwing sickies and no wonder. For gamers who have waited 13 years, this is the equivalent of a football World Cup

If there were an unusual number of people missing from your workplace at the back end of this week, they may have come down with GTA flu. You don’t need to be a video game person to have heard that there’s a new instalment of Grand Theft Auto, the enormously popular series in which you drive around sprawling American cities committing crimes. It has been all over the news. And if you are not a video game person, maybe that seems baffling. Why is this game such a big deal?

Let me assure you that this is no ordinary video game release. The last GTA instalment, GTA V, came out in 2013, so fans have waited 13 years fo
title: Did you come down with GTA flu? I won’t judge – I may even join you in Vice City | Imogen West-Knights

author: David Conn
description:
Prof Peter Hindmarsh played key role in conviction of two Birmingham parents whose son died after diabetes episode

A doctor who gave expert evidence that helped to convict Lucy Letby, and who was barred during the trial from treating patients, was then instructed as an expert witness in another prosecution.

The Guardian revealed this week that Prof Peter Hindmarsh was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023, during the main trial of Letby, by his employer, University College London hospitals trust (UCLH). The jury, who five months later convicted Letby of the murder of seven babies, were never told.

Continue reading...
title: Letby trial doctor barred from treating patients was expert witness in another case

author: Rob Smyth
description:
• Updates from the T20 international at the MCG in Melbourne

  • Play starts at 7.15pm AEDT/8.15am GMT | Send us a mail

After a toe-curling, stonewalling press conference before the recent one-day series against England, Australia’s usually happy-go-lucky T20 captain, Mitch Marsh, opted out of a repeat before the Twenty20s that start here on Saturday.

In his place came Victoria’s Sam Harper to talk about his looming debut at the MCG. A nice local angle, for sure, with the 29-year-old wicketkeeper having overcome some troubling concussions in the past. But also a touch optimistic if intended to switch the focus in Australia away from the sandpaper skip fire.

Continue reading...
title: Australia v England: first men’s T20 cricket international – live

author: Catherine Shoard
description:
For three hours, Nathan Fielder opts not to quiz convicted criminal Elizabeth Holmes on the details of her deception. Instead, he looks into her eyes and asks if she’s for real. Is that why his film has been so successful?

• This article does not contain major spoilers

Sometimes, people who have lied lie about whether or not they’ve lied. They even, on occasion, fail to tell the truth despite having sworn to do so – in court, for instance, or staring deeply into the eyes of someone who is sitting right there.

Is that a shock? Probably not. We all engage in versions of such behaviour every day. We understand that the current climate of mutually clueless echo chambers helps claptrap gain traction. But we can still recognise the difference between little white lies and big red flags. We know that the moment anyone starts using the phrase “my truth” it’s time to cancel the wedding.
title: You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth

author: Rupert Jones
description:
With living costs set to rise higher in 2027, here’s how you can help your savings and pension keep up with soaring prices

For many of us, it is when we go to the supermarket that we really notice the impact of inflation. The trolley-load of groceries that used to cost £80 has broken the £100 barrier, and some of the packets look smaller than they were.

But inflation also acts as an invisible stealth tax on savings cash, silently taking a bite out of many people’s nest-eggs. When it is running high, the odds are that your savings are being eroded.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Like an invisible stealth tax’: ways to shield your cash from UK inflation

author: Gwilym Mumford
description:
In this week’s newsletter: It could be the biggest entertainment release ever, but its reach reveals the limit of shared cultural experience

An estimated cost of $1bn. A development period of 13 years. A production team of 5,000 people. A game map the size of Manchester. An estimated 24m copies sold through pre-orders and launch day alone, generating $2.36bn. Thousands upon thousands of days of leave booked and sick days taken to play the thing, costing the US economy an estimated $1bn (yep, another billion figure) in lost productivity. The scale of Grand Theft Auto VI – and the tidal wave of facts and figures surrounding its making and economic impact – truly boggles the mind.

Even if you, like me, are unlikely to ever sit down and play the thing, you will struggle to escape its influence. Footage both sinister and benign – from graphic shooting sprees to mellow clips of its protagonists strolling, hand in hand, down the beach – will follow you around Facebook, Instagr
title: The Guide #270: Grand Theft Auto VI is everywhere – but is it really the cultural event of the decade?

author: Lola Akinmade Åkerström
description:
Swedes adore the festive season, embracing the shorter days with fairy lights, yuletide feasts and fun in the snow

I’ll let you in on a secret: I often tell people that summer is the best time to visit Stockholm. Clouds drift across impossibly blue skies, we skip around midsummer maypoles singing folk songs and cruise the waterways, bobbing and weaving through the archipelago’s 30,000-plus islands.

That’s mostly because I want to keep December in Stockholm to myself. Soft white snow dusts buildings of ochre and burnt sienna like icing on a cake. Festive candles light up pavements leading to cosy cafes, where the earthy, buttery smell of seasonal saffron buns (lussekatter) replaces cinnamon buns for fika, our revered tradition of coffee and cake.

Continue reading...
title: Why I love Stockholm in winter: ‘A return to slowing down, cosying up and revering every glimmer of light’

author: Rhik Samadder
description:
If you’re a cyberpunk who loves ennui and watching actors you can’t see speak words you can’t hear, get stuck in! The rest of us will just be baffled and bored

Why is James Bond not a TV series by now? Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings, Alien, Star Wars – all given the TV treatment. Franchise-mining is fantastic business, maximising attention share in order to sell adverts. So why not Bond, which is co-owned by Amazon? Maybe watching a punchy sex addict every week, saying his name with weirdly administrative syntax, might just be … too much?

I entertained these thoughts while struggling to get through another series expansion: Blade Runner 2099 (Prime Video, from Wednesday). I’m a fan of the films. Before the original, cinema had imagined the future as serene and orderly. Blade Runner introduced many of us to novelist Philip K Dick’s vision, in which tech has colonised every aspect of life, but inequality has got worse. Surveillance, artificial beings and unchecked c
title: Blade Runner 2099: fans will have no idea what is happening in this sci-fi sequel. Why is it even on TV?

author: Emilija Morrison
description:
The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security

  • Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

What child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.”

Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy.

Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism
title: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious | Emilija Morrison

author: Jackson Boxer
description:
This dessert makes me feel like I’m in Sicily again

Ice-cream holds an irresistible allure for me. That combination of richness, lightness, and the pure, sensual pleasure of it melting gently across the palate maintains an unbreakable hold over my imagination. In fact, other than fruit, it’s the only sweet food with which I have a genuine emotional relationship: I can remember many ice-creams I’ve eaten incredibly vividly, and in a way I just don’t with almost all other desserts and pastries. Today’s ice is a case in point, having been developed from a memory of an almond gelato eaten in Sicily just after the annual harvest.

Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House, Vesper and Dove, all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and
title: Jackson Boxer’s vegan recipe for almond sorbet with grape granita

author: Oliver Southall
description:
Hurstpierpoint, West Sussex: The way that it sits patiently, and solves problems … it’s hard not to wonder if it has some kind of inner life

Three months with a newborn has given me a fresh perspective on nature. What will Tom enjoy out here, I wonder, as we step outside. I hold him under trees and watch his astonished eyes. Every morning, as a hopeful inoculation against arachnophobia, I show him the garden spider (Araneus diadematus) outside our back window. Is that a smile?

Attending to a baby’s developing preferences has got me thinking about what makes an individual creature unique. Recently I learned that Len Howard – whose 1952 book Birds As Individuals lovingly described the quirks of her garden tits and thrushes – lived
title: Country diary: Watching a garden spider at work – do I detect a personality? | Oliver Southall

author: Dee Jefferson
description:
In the Museum of Contemporary Art, the French artist’s first major Australian show is truly unpredictable – influenced by real-time data coming from a Spanish farm

I’m standing in a massive white-cube space, staring at a perplexing assortment of objects. There are several expensive looking lamps; a massive industrial fan; a couple of speakers; marquee-style lights; a glowing assemblage of power adapters. At the back of the gallery, a silvery light slides up and down a pole. The bulbs are flickering erratically, and there’s a low hum of machine noise, overlaid with bird song and distant barking.

As an installation, taken by itself, it’s deceptively underwhelming – a spectacle without a story.

title: In a Sydney gallery, Philippe Parreno’s art is powered by a desert 17,000km away
